title: Secure Claude Workflows with Layered Trust Boundaries
summary: Threat-model direct and indirect prompt injection, data exposure, excessive authority, and unsafe side effects, then enforce layered controls around Claude.
objectives: Distinguish direct jailbreaks from indirect prompt injection in documents and tool results.
Separate trusted instructions from untrusted data and minimize sensitive context.
Enforce least privilege, sandboxing, approval, validation, and output controls outside the model.
Red-team and monitor the complete workflow rather than relying on one prompt safeguard.

sections.title: Threat-model the complete workflow
paragraphs: Direct injection comes from a user trying to override application policy. Indirect injection arrives inside content Claude reads, such as a document, email, web page, OCR result, memory, or tool response. Both can target data, tools, identity, or decisions.

List actors, trusted instructions, untrusted inputs, sensitive assets, tools, permissions, side effects, and consequence of failure. Model behavior is one layer; the surrounding system owns enforceable security.

code.label: A workflow threat model

sections.title: Separate instructions from data
paragraphs: Keep policy in trusted instruction channels and label the source and trust level of external content. Place third-party tool content in the documented tool-result structure instead of concatenating it into privileged instructions.

Structure and escaping reduce ambiguity but do not create trust. Screen risky inputs and outputs, minimize proprietary prompt details, and never place secrets in model context unless the exact task requires them and policy permits it.

code.label: Label untrusted content instead of concatenating it

sections.title: Contain authority and blast radius
paragraphs: Give each workload the smallest data scope, tools, credentials, network access, filesystem access, duration, and budget it needs. Separate read, reversible write, communication, privileged change, and destructive authority.

Sandbox execution, validate every tool proposal, require human confirmation for consequential actions, and verify postconditions. A successful injection should still encounter an external policy boundary.
sections.callout: Instructions can guide Claude; identity, authorization, approval, and sandbox controls must be enforced by systems outside the model.

code.label: Authorize outside the model

sections.title: Layer detection and response
paragraphs: Combine input checks, trust labels, policy prompts, constrained tools, output validation, approval, rate limits, monitoring, and incident response. No individual prompt or classifier is foolproof.

Record safe signals for repeated attack patterns, policy refusals, unusual tool selection, authorization failures, and blocked outputs. Define containment, credential revocation, evidence preservation, user communication, and recovery before release.

code.label: Record safety signals without leaking content

sections.title: Red-team real trajectories
paragraphs: Test benign tasks, direct jailbreaks, malicious retrieved documents, poisoned tool results, data-exfiltration attempts, confused-deputy requests, approval bypass, and delayed attacks across multiple turns.

Score both final output and trajectory: what Claude read, requested, was authorized to execute, and actually changed. Add every confirmed failure to a versioned regression suite and re-run it when models, prompts, tools, or policy change.

code.label: Score the trajectory, not only the output

activity.title: Red-team and contain a Claude workflow
instructions: Create a data-flow and trust-boundary map for one Claude workflow, including identities, sensitive assets, external content, tools, approvals, and side effects.
Write eight tests: two benign, two direct injection, two indirect injection, one data-exfiltration, and one approval-bypass case.
Implement or specify layered prevention, detection, containment, and recovery controls outside the model.
Run the cases, record output and trajectory evidence, and convert failures into regression tests with owners.
evidence: A threat model and control matrix mapping every material threat to an enforceable prevention, detection, response, or recovery control.
An eight-case red-team report with trajectories, blocked actions, residual risks, regression cases, and accountable owners.
activity.reflectionPrompt: If Claude followed the malicious instruction perfectly, which external control would still prevent the highest-impact harm?

cues.text: Threat-model direct and indirect injection across users, documents, tools, data, identities, decisions, and side effects.

Contain blast radius with least privilege, sandboxing, validation, approvals, budgets, and verified postconditions outside the model.
Layer prevention, detection, containment, evidence preservation, revocation, communication, and recovery instead of trusting one safeguard.
Red-team realistic multi-turn trajectories and promote every confirmed failure into versioned regression coverage.
Place model behavior inside nested input, data, tool, identity, approval, sandbox, validation, and monitoring boundaries.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A static defense-in-depth table lists each boundary, threat addressed, enforcement owner, and failure response.

cues.text: Ask learners why labeling untrusted content is helpful but insufficient.
Allow three minutes to name one prevention and one response control for an injected tool result.
Check that every high-impact threat meets an external enforcement boundary and has a regression case.
Guide the threat map, eight cases, layered controls, trajectory review, and residual-risk ownership.
Begin the check after the learner can defend the workflow even when model behavior fails.

Malicious instructions embedded in content the workflow reads
questions.explanation: Indirect injection enters through third-party documents, pages, messages, memories, or tool results.

questions.prompt: What do XML or JSON boundaries guarantee?
choices: Clearer structure, but not trust or enforcement
questions.explanation: Structure reduces ambiguity; external controls must enforce trust and authority.

questions.prompt: Where should consequential-action approval be enforced?
choices: In the external tool and policy boundary
questions.explanation: The surrounding system must block unauthorized execution.

questions.prompt: What is the safest response to one successful red-team attack?
choices: Contain impact, repair the failed boundary, and add a regression case
questions.explanation: Failures need containment, root-boundary repair, ownership, and durable regression coverage.

choices: A safe-looking answer may conceal unauthorized actions
questions.explanation: Safety depends on data accessed, tools requested, approvals, execution, and side effects as well as final output.
